reviewed.by: PENDING — gates not yet run. STANDING CONSTRAINTS: (1) Never say archaeology 'proves the Bible' — library/archaeology.html opens by calling that leap a mistake, and scene 14 is the honest bound that keeps this reel inside the essay. (2) Never say no archaeological find has ever contradicted a biblical claim — that is a retired claim (2026-07-28 pocket-card gate). (3) The Belshazzar finds establish the MAN and his AUTHORITY, not the date of Daniel or the events it narrates — the essay states this explicitly and scene 13 carries it. (4) Do not claim critics doubted Pontius Pilate's existence — he is attested by Tacitus, Josephus and Philo; the Pilate Stone is the principal contemporary EPIGRAPHIC evidence, which is a different and smaller claim. (5) 'On the likely sense of Daniel 5:16' — the third-place reading is the natural one but the essay hedges it, so the reel says 'the natural reading' and never 'the only'.

voiceover: For a long time, one name in the Bible had no evidence at all. Daniel chapter five tells of a feast in Babylon, a hand writing on the wall, and a king named Belshazzar. The problem was that no other source knew him. The Babylonian king lists ended the dynasty with a king called Nabonidus. The Greek historians agreed. There was no Belshazzar anywhere. So critics drew the obvious conclusion: the author of Daniel did not know Babylon. He had invented a king. It was treated as the giveaway — the mistake that showed the book was written late, by someone far from the events. Then the clay tablets were read. A cylinder of Nabonidus names his eldest son. Bel-shar-usur. Belshazzar. And the Babylonian records say something stranger still. Nabonidus was not in Babylon. He spent years at Tema, in Arabia, and he entrusted the kingship to his son. So Belshazzar was real, and he was ruling — but he was not the king. His father was. Now go back to Daniel five. The king offers a reward to anyone who can read the writing. And what he offers is oddly specific: to be made the third ruler in the kingdom. Not second. Third. On the natural reading, that is because the first two places were already taken — by Nabonidus, and by Belshazzar himself. A detail that made no sense for centuries turns out to fit a political arrangement nobody knew about. Be careful what this does and does not show. It establishes the man and his authority. It does not by itself settle when Daniel was written, or the events it narrates. Archaeology does not prove the Bible, and anyone who tells you it does is overselling. What it does is this: it keeps answering, on details no forger would think to invent.

lines.t: but he was not the king.
A detail that made no sense
